title: Community
hookLine: a meeting that gets loud, and the Vajjis' conditions for a community that lasts (DN 16)
tomorrow: the tired stranger across from you on the bus. what's their story?

lines: WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT THIS WAY.
A KING ASKS ABOUT THE VAJJIS.
cards: Every group has the meeting. The club, the team, the congregation, the family chat about the holidays. One side says we've always done it this way, and that's why it works.
The other says that's exactly why nobody new comes anymore. Voices rise. Someone threatens to quit.
The Buddha had a view on what keeps a community alive, and it begins with a king planning a war.
In the last journey of the Buddha's life, a king sends a minister to ask whether he can conquer the Vajjis, a confederation of clans.

teach.b: The Buddha doesn't answer the minister directly. He turns to Ananda and asks: do the Vajjis meet often?
Do they meet in harmony, and rise in harmony, and do their business in harmony?

teach.h: KEEP IT ALL, OR LEAVE ROOM?
teach.b: Do they keep their old ways, not making new rules or throwing out the established ones? Do they honor their elders? While they do these things, he says, expect them to grow, not decline.
Then he gives the monks their own version. So here are two voices inside the tradition, each at its best.
The first: keep the old ways. Not abolishing what was laid down is right there on the list.

Tradition says that after the Buddha's death, the elders at the first council couldn't agree which small rules might be dropped, so they kept them all, and a shared form has held communities together ever since.
The second: the same sutta records the Buddha saying that after he's gone, the sangha may set aside the lesser and minor rules if it wishes. He left room.
A community that can't adapt can lose the people it's meant to serve. Teachers and schools still weigh these differently.
But notice what comes first on the list, before any question of old or new: meet often, and meet in harmony. Disagree in the room. Leave it together.

how: Buddhist monastic communities meet regularly, including the uposatha observance days, and lay communities gather at temples and centers for practice, festivals and decisions.

o: people who keep meeting, in harmony, even when they disagree
whoever happens to live in the same town as you
a group that agrees on everything and never argues

games.q: the conditions for a community — tap the pairs.
p: the clans a king wanted to conquer
the first thing the Buddha asks about
meet, rise and do business together
may be set aside, the sutta says

s: the Buddha said a community must never change a single rule
the same sutta records him allowing the sangha to set aside lesser and minor rules.
the Buddha's first question about the Vajjis is whether they meet often
meeting often, and in harmony, comes before anything about old or new.

games.q: your temple's youth group wants to move the old festival to a weekend so more friends can come. the elders object. state the elders' best case.
o: old people just dislike change; there's nothing more to it.
a shared form handed down holds people together; keeping it is part of the harmony.
the festival belongs to the elders, so the youth should simply obey.
games.why: that's the 'keep it all' voice at its best: not abolishing what was laid down is one of the conditions. the other voice can point to the Buddha leaving room.

practice: Bring to mind one gathering you belong to, or could: a team, a class, a temple, a dinner table. Picture the next time it meets.
Picture yourself there, arriving on time, listening to the person you usually disagree with, and leaving on good terms.

wordCard.voice: Community: in the Buddha's words to Ananda, people who meet often, meet in harmony, and rise together.

orig.note: Pali: united, in harmony; the word for how the Vajjis meet and rise.

carryVoice: For your pocket: meet in harmony, even when you don't agree. Five of six on friends and community.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta: Vassakara's visit; the Vajjis' conditions of non-decline: meeting often, meeting and rising in harmony, keeping established ways, honoring elders; the same applied to the monks; permission to abolish the lesser and minor rules)
Vinaya, Cullavagga XI (the first council: the elders cannot agree which rules are minor and keep them all)
